utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Case number IT-00-39 & 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'll hear the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Judge May. Assisting me today is Alan Tieger, to my immediate right, and to his right Mr. Thomas Hannis, and to my left Ms. Carmela Annink-Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You better say who you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mark Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Deyan Brashich for the Krajisnik Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Robert Pavich, Peter Murphy, and Eugene O'Sullivan for the Plavsic defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a Status Conference to determine the progress being made. The first matter, and I'll hear the parties on the matters they consider relevant in due course, but the matter which the Trial Chamber would be particularly concerned to do would be to fix a date for the final pre-trial brief for the Prosecution, fix a date for Defence pre-trial briefs with a view to a trial in the autumn. Mr. Harmon, you can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Judge May, we have had a number of Rule 65 ter conferences, and we have, at the last 65 ter conference, which was held on the 6th of February, 2002, the parties met and discussed a variety of items. One of the items which came up was a proposed schedule, and the schedule that had been proposed to us by Ms. Featherstone was that the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief be completed and submitted by the end of April, with a Defence pre-trial brief at the end of July, and a Pre-Trial Conference in early September. That was a schedule that we have considered and discussed amongst ourselves, the Prosecution bench, and we can meet that schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. The end of April. In fact, the 30th of April is a holiday. I'll be reminded if the 1st of May is a court day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The 2nd of May, I'm told, is the first available date. So we'll order the final brief, list of witnesses and exhibits 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before I turn to the Defence, are there any matters which you would wish to raise, Mr. Harmon, or are there any matters which the Trial Chamber should be apprised of? I know there are ongoing problems and ongoing discussions between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I know Your Honour has been fully apprised of the discussions and the undertakings that have been made by the parties in the course of the Rule 65 ter conferences. One issue that has been raised repeatedly is when we will file our Rule 92 bis submissions to the Chamber, and as Your Honour may well be aware, I undertook to file within 14 days of a decision on our application for the amended consolidated indictment I would make such a filing, and I have had some discussions, albeit very brief discussions, with my colleagues from the Defence from Plavsic team about their ability to comply with that undertaking that I have made. Now, I will tell you and I will defer to my colleagues to explain the reasons that they have, but I'm willing to file a 92 bis submission within the time period I said that I would, but I have submitted to the Defence as well a list of witness statements for which we're seeking admission under 92 bis (B) and (D). I've submitted that schedule to the Defence. It is my understanding that the Defence intends to examine that list and will in good faith report to me which of those statements are acceptable and which are not and give me the reasons why. It may not be the complete list, but they will take a good faith effort -- make a good faith effort at complying with that deadline, and I am certainly amenable to be flexible myself on the undertaking that we have made. If the Defence has some concerns and some issues that relate to some of these issues, I will defer my filing of the 92 bis filing. So I think, Your Honour, that issue on the first and large number of potential witnesses for which 92 bis written evidence can be admitted has certainly been addressed by the parties. The witnesses, the majority of those witnesses, the substantial majority of those witnesses, have been identified and the statements have been produced. There remain approximately, at this point in time, 30 additional witness statements for which we're in the process of obtaining attestations and, therefore, there can be no submission as to those 92 bis statements. I say that the number 30 is an approximation. That's the first matter I'd like to bring to Your Honour's attention. In addition, there have been discussions throughout the pre-trial proceedings as to other events that would be triggered by the Rule -- by the decision of the Trial Chamber on the amended indictment. One of those relates to adjudicated facts. And we have submitted -- I think the last time we submitted - we, the Prosecution - submitted a list of adjudicated facts was in November, and I understood the Defence objection that until they had the opportunity to see the charging instrument in its final form, they were not in a position to respond to our request to agree on certain adjudicated facts. We have now received the decision of the Trial Chamber on the amended indictment, and therefore, I think we will be able to proceed fairly quickly on a submission that relates to adjudicated facts. There also is the issue of the expert witness statements that have been submitted. There were approximately 14 of those statements filed by the office of the Prosecutor, and of those 14, there were black and white photographs in 11 of those -- ten of those submissions, and I received a request from my colleagues from the Defence that those photographs were not of sufficient quality to be examined by the Defence expert who was examining the exhumation reports. There was a request made to me to get colour photographs in lieu of the black and white photographs and submit those to the Defence. I received, pursuant to that request, one set of colour photographs. I haven't had the time to show them to the Defence. There are approximately a thousand photographs. I'm going to be reproducing those photographs and making them available to the Defence. And there are three reports, expert reports, that I filed that have no photographs whatsoever. Now, it's my understanding that the expert who has -- the joint Defence expert who is analysing the expert submissions made by us has completed his report, and therefore I expect to receive, unless I hear something to the contrary, some information about the acceptability of at least three of those Rule 94 bis reports. The issue of translations, of course, we are continuing to grapple with. My colleague Mr. Tieger is in a position to report on an initiative that we have made in respect of trying to ameliorate the problem of untranslated documents. We are pleased that the initiative that has been undertaken is in a position to proceed forthwith. And I will defer, if Your Honour pleases, to my colleague Mr. Tieger, who can at least report to Your Honour on the status of that initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm pleased to bring this matter again to the Court's attention. As you know, it was raised once in the 65 ter conference. It was followed up by a specific proposal which was brought to the attention of the Court. As you may know, it emerged from discussions between the Defence and the Prosecution, and I'm heartened that the response from the Defence has been a positive one. In sum, this proposal is as follows: The Prosecution will submit to the Defence draft or unofficial translations of documents. That means documents that were prepared either by CLSS but have not been yet produced in final form, or documents -- document translations produced by language assistants who are not technically a part of CLSS. Thereupon, the Defence will review those documents within a specified time period and return them to the Prosecution, advising whether or not the translation as provided is acceptable or whether or not the Defence wishes to see certain revisions. At that point, the Prosecution will have the document, will also have the specified period of time within which to respond. If there is no agreement at that stage, the documents will then be submitted to CLSS for resolution of the dispute. Now, clearly that procedure depends upon resources. Before making the proposal formally, I discussed this matter with the Registry. The Registry has agreed to provide the Defence with two translators each for purposes of this review, as part of what will amount, I believe, to a pilot project. I believe that all of us hope and expect that with the success of the initial phase of this project, that the resources devoted to it will expand, making available to all of us a pool of translation resources previously unavailable for this purpose and hopefully breaking the translation logjam. As I mentioned, I've discussed the proposal further with the Defence. It appears to me, based on those discussions, that the only remaining issues are those of mechanics, precisely the details of implementing the proposal rather than the benefit and value of the proposal in theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that can be done administratively rather than by the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Harmon, are there any other areas to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There was the difficult question of the videos, I seem to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There is an issue of videos that I was expecting to further discuss with my colleague, Mr. Brashich, but the issue of the videos was that there was certainly a number of videos that we had submitted to the Defence, and some of these videos did not have transcripts. And at the -- I believe it was the February -- or two 65 ter conferences ago there was an assurance that the transcript work would be provided by the 1st of February, and since then I haven't had time to talk to Mr. Brashich. I have not received any of those transcripts. I have obviously made an inquiry as to at some point in time receiving at least the work of progress, the works that had been completed up to the point of February 1st, even if the complete project is not complete. So yes, there has been a discussion as to the videos, and I'm told there has been some work done on those transcripts, but Mr. Brashich and I have not had an opportunity to meet prior to coming here today, to clarify what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I'll hear from the Defence. Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I am mindful of the comments made by the Court with regard to May 2, with regard to the final pre-trial brief, and I've listened to the comments by my colleague in the Prosecution's office, and I agree with some of his submissions and positions and disagree with others. The first issue that was raised, Your Honour, was the 92 bis statements. I wrote to Mr. Harmon this morning and advised him that I would, within the time constraints that the Trial Chamber has made, would act upon the list of proposed witnesses and advise which we will oppose and seek cross-examination. With regard to the adjudicated facts, my predecessor has gone over at least a portion - or so it has been reported back to me - of the adjudicated facts, and I believe that within recent memory of man, the First World War, the prior adjudicated facts can be agreed upon. The rest I'm willing to address with Mr. Harmon. With regard to the expert witness statements, I received a memorandum from Mr. Harmon that it was his understanding at the last 65 ter conference that we had, that the expert witness that the Defence, both the Defences had retained, had completed his work. That is just not so. It awaits those thousand-some-odd photographs in colour. With regard to the three expert witness statements which did not contain any photographs, I'm due to be in Belgrade tomorrow. I will check on it and report back. If they're finished, of course I'll turn them over to the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger speaks about the translations. We had some communication with regard to translations. Mr. Tieger reported as to his discussions with the Registry and this idea of four translators working with the Defence. I had inquired some 20, 25 days ago as to the mechanics. I have not had a reply to that, so I cannot report to the Trial Chamber the Krajisnik Defence position on the translators. With regard to the videos and transcripts, in the last Status Conference, or two Status Conferences ago, where I was physically present, I advised Ms. Featherstone that it had come to a dead stop. The transcripts are no longer being prepared or done. And I'll get back to that issue. I had sent Ms. Featherstone in Chambers, in advance of this particular Status Conference, a suggested number of questions that should be directed to the Prosecution. I have not had a response from Chambers, and I presume that those questions were not passed on to the Prosecution. This again ties in with the translations. At least from the point of view of the Krajisnik Defence, we do not know at this point in time exactly how many additional documents remain untranslated and when the translation, assuming both the joint effort with the four translators or without that joint effort, will be done. Now, with regard to the July date for the Defence to submit its pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm open to argument, of course, about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Judge, the position the Krajisnik Defence finds itself in at this point. Under the regime that exists, the Registry has designated this case as a Category 1 case; most serious. And Krajisnik Defence, before I got involved, was allotted a certain amount of hours and time. We have used up those hours. At this present time, the Krajisnik Defence comprises of me, one clerical assistant, and two investigators. That's all that we have in the budget. I am in discussions with the Registry to make to us available additional resources. I had requested of the Registry to inquire of the Prosecution how many full-time attorneys are employed by the Prosecution, how many paralegals, and other resources the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's short circuit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's short circuit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm finishing, Your Honour. I'm putting the Court on notice that unless we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Finish the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I was going to raise with you -- I'm not stopping you. When I say, "Let's short circuit it," you don't have a co-counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Now, to finish my thought, Your Honour, I have consulted with my client, and we have spoken long and hard about it. Unless I can see that my professional responsibilities with regard to Mr. Krajisnik and the enormity of this case can be met, I'm going to make the motion to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. withdraw, because I'm not going to put Mr. Krajisnik's life in jeopardy by not being able to give him the full attention and support that I need in his defence. But that is still under negotiations with the Registry, but I just wanted to place the Trial Chamber on notice that there is a possibility of a change in counsel or no counsel, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, your responsibility is to Mr. Krajisnik. You have undertaken his defence for a year or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is, of course, important that you have the resources available. No doubt there's a reason why you don't have co-counsel, but I don't know what it is. I would expect you to have co-counsel in a case of this sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Further than that, I don't think it's necessary to go at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But supposing you have the resources, how long are you asking for for a pre-trial brief? Bearing in mind the necessity of getting this case on to trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: I'm bearing that very much in mind, Your Honour, especially since my client is in gaol. If that were not a factor, I would seek more time. However, I think because my client is in gaol, that I think July 30th is an unworkable date, especially in light of summer recesses, and I would ask for September 1, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavich.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I have little to add to what's already been presented to the Court this afternoon. Two points, I think, though, are worth making and highlighting since they've already been made in part. First, we do expect to do everything that we can to comply with whatever schedules the Court presents us. Toward that end, we've been working diligently with the Prosecution in order to meet the various deadlines that we anticipate and that we've already been given. There have been two major obstacles in our cooperative effort. One, of course, as the Court is well aware, is the translation problem. The other is problems that have arisen with regard to the ability of the Prosecution to provide disclosure relating to reciprocal discovery and to Rule 68 matters. My colleague Mr. O'Sullivan has been in intensive discussions over the past several days with the Prosecution, and I would ask that I be allowed to defer to him with regard to these matters, with the leave of the Court, so that he can explain the status of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll also respond to several other matters. First, 92 bis statements and the -- our position on those statements. Mr. Harmon's quite correct that we are in a position now to begin that process with the Prosecution. There will be, in the short-term, statements to which we can agree and will not seek leave to cross-examine. There are, however, a second category of witnesses where we are seeking deferral until the filing of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief so that we will be in a position where we are comfortable to say either way whether we will seek leave for cross-examination or not. But having said that, there are at this time a good number of statements where we can agree with the Prosecution to fast track 92 bis statement process. I might add, however, that some of the 92 bis statements are still in the B/C/S language and the translation problem is rearing its head again in regard to those statements, but in that context, we can move forward. The same applies, Your Honour, in regard to adjudicated facts. We are in a position immediately to meet with the Prosecution and agree on some and identify where we dispute with the Prosecution on others. There are some matters that have come out of the most recent Rule 65 ter conference on February 7th with the legal officer, and I think it's important that we present those to you, Your Honour, from our perspective and indicate how we see this as being problematic in the preparation of this trial. First the expert witnesses. The Prosecution has stated that he has a demographics expert, a propaganda expert, a constitutional law expert, and an administrative law expert. We have not received expert reports from any of those witnesses. I hasten to add that we've been made aware that these witnesses are on the Prosecution witness list since August 31st. We would expect that, given the nature of the complexity we can anticipate of their expert reports, that the sooner we get those the better, and we've been waiting months now for them. The second matter or category of witnesses that arises out of the last 65 ter are what we've been calling the international witnesses. Those are people from international organisations or government representatives. The Prosecution says he has 14 more such statements to disclose to us. In our submission, the Prosecution has a duty under Rule 66 to disclose statements from those people when he knows that he intends to call them. And he has identified 14, apparently. We don't know who they are, and we haven't yet received statements in connection with those potential witnesses. On the issue of translation, we share Mr. Tieger's enthusiasm for the pilot project. I do want to put this in perspective, however. To date, we have received 9.689 documents from the Prosecution as disclosure under Rule 65 ter or the ongoing process of the pre-trial brief disclosure. Our best estimate is that between 50 and 60 per cent of those documents are not translated. That means, Your Honour, between 4.800 and 5.600 documents. And I can tell you it's daunting in the least to stand in front of a wall of over 5.000 documents that are not in a language that you understand, that are considered by the Prosecution to be relevant to its case and not be able to examine those documents or understand them, let alone digest them and fit them into our anticipated response to the Prosecution's case. It is most daunting, Your Honour. The videos, as Your Honour's aware, I'm sure, from our last 65 ter meeting, we are a long way from being prepared to be able to work with those videos. There are over 366 video sequences. Approximately 82 have been transcribed. Over 280 need translation. It's a similar problem to the 5.000 untranslated documents. They're in a language that we cannot use. I turn to reciprocal discovery and the timing of reciprocal discovery in the context of the timetable we're envisaging. The Prosecution has said that they are expecting to meet a reciprocal discovery deadline in March, and we fully anticipate receiving much of a request that we made in December this month. We have, however, been informed that one collection of documents in possession of the Prosecution cannot be disclosed to us until May 31st. Now, we don't know the quantity of documents, and again, we don't know necessarily which language these documents will be in. Your Honour knows that we've been working constructively with the Prosecution in our endeavours to facilitate reciprocal disclosure, but it has come to our attention and we believe that the fact that the Prosecution can provide no index of its categorisation of its documents -- we submitted to the Prosecution for such an index to help us determine their organisational principle so that we could set specific parameters on our requests. Your Honour, we're dealing with the trial of a political leader whose guilt or innocence will be determined in large part by documents. That is why we need these documents. And finally, and lastly in regards to reciprocal discovery is Rule 70. Mr. Harmon has informed us that some of the documents we've requested on reciprocal discovery are protected by Rule 70 and that he has requested the provider to lift the confidentiality. But again, timing is of the essence. Once the request is made to that provider, it's out of the party's hands, and we have to wait for a response from that provider. And again, quantity of documents is unknown to us, the language in which they will be -- in which they're prepared is unknown to us. And I wish to reiterate that in a political leadership case, when we make a submission for reciprocal discovery for materials which we think are material to our defence, it's important that we have them to prepare our defence. So those are still the obstacles there, Your Honour. Some of them are institutional. Some of them are beyond the control of the parties. But the fact of the matter is it impacts directly on our ability to prepare and to respond in a timely way. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Pavich, is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. With respect to the question that you put to Mr. Brashich, I think our response would be that it's very difficult for us to give the Court an assessment, an intelligent assessment, of when we will be in a position to provide our pre-trial brief. It may be that we will have to look at the material that will be forthcoming in April or on 2 May from the Prosecution and that at that time we'll, for the first time, be able to give the Court an intelligent assessment of when we believe we will be able to provide a product that will be worthy of the Court's attention. In lieu of the fact that -- well, with respect to that, I would suggest that Mr. Brashich's deadline at this point or his suggestion of 1 September is realistic, but we probably won't be able to make a firm commitment to that until the materials that have been outlined at this point that we're awaiting, that Mr. O'Sullivan has indicated are still out there that we haven't seen, are made available to us, both with respect to the translations of documents which the Prosecution intends to use and as to those documents that would be covered under reciprocal discovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I shall make the order for the Defence pre-trial brief for the 1st of September. It seems to me that that is realistic, given the date of the Prosecution final brief, four months. I hear what Mr. Pavic says, but it's important that this trial do be brought on rather than waiting longer, and therefore this is an important step towards it. Dealing with the matters which Mr. O'Sullivan raised, he raised questions about the Prosecution expert reports and the international witness statements. Can you assist with that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge May, I certainly can. In respect of the international witnesses, the reason the Defence hasn't received some of those statements is because they're protected by Rule 70 at this point, and we are awaiting the provider authority to disclose those statements. Some statements are works that are still statements being taken, so the statements have not been completed. In respect of the expert witnesses, some of these experts have not yet been selected, and therefore no reports exist. Now, we have filed a number of expert reports. I have made it clear before Your Honour and to the Defence that subject to very sensitive experts for some issues, we intend to provide, as soon as we can and as soon as we get the expert reports and as soon as they're completed, we'll provide those to the Defence. That's an undertaking we have made in the past. We stand by that undertaking. But we have not completed, in some cases, the process of the identification of the particular witness or the completion of some expert reports. Now, some expert reports -- I can give you an example. Some expert reports deal with -- are very, very difficult in the short term to complete because of conditions that exist in theatre. I don't care to expand on that now. I can explain that to Ms. Featherstone. I have, in fact, mentioned it once to Ms. Featherstone. I can explain it to my colleagues. But we will complete these reports as quickly as we can, and we will provide them to the Defence. Now, Mr. O'Sullivan mentioned the Rule 92 bis statements and his undertaking to complete, as soon as possible, a review of those statements. To assist the Defence, I provided them with a document that identified the number of witnesses, the category of whether we are going to be seeking admission in terms of a written statement or in terms of a transcript from a previous proceeding, or both. These witnesses - there are 95 - they are all crime-base witnesses. These are all people who support the crime elements in the cases itself. They are not international witnesses, they are not expert witnesses, they are not background witnesses. In respect of the videos, let me provide Your Honour with the statistics that we have in respect of that. The total number of videos that we've disclosed to the Defence are 18 videos. There are 316 sequences disclosed, 205 transcripts have been disclosed, and there are 82 translations have been disclosed. My colleague Mr. Brashich mentioned in the course of this hearing that the expert was no longer able to complete the work that was done in respect of transcribing those videotape sequences. Your Honour, that may be the case, but the sooner we can get the transcripts of the video sequences that have been completed, the better, and we would ask that Your Honour direct the Defence to provide those to us, because there is a process of dealing with those transcriptions. We have to review them for their accuracy, we have to then submit for proper translation those video sequences that have been now transcribed properly. So while at the last Status Conference Mr. Brashich informed Ms. Featherstone that the work had stopped, we certainly are anxious to receive the work that had been completed up to that point in time. It would advance, very frankly, this process of discovery and advance our efforts in respect of identifying the videotapes that will be used ultimately in evidence. In respect of a reciprocal discovery, yes, my colleague Mr. O'Sullivan did accurately describe that there was one collection that was a problem for us. What the procedure has been has been that the Defence has identified for us categories of documents they want to receive. We have pursued identifying and collecting those documents and we have submitted to the Defence a significant number of documents responsive to the categories that they have identified. We undertook to provide to the Defence the remaining documents by the 31st of March, and we will provide to -- there are three collections left that need to be reviewed for those responsive documents. I was informed today that yesterday there was a problem with an optical scanning portion of the operation that related to one collection, and therefore we were not in a position to provide the one collection to them at the date that we had promised to provide it to them. The remaining two categories we will provide -- we will review and complete our review and will provide to the Defence by the 2nd of April. So I think that is obviously significant and substantial compliance with what the Defence has requested. In respect of Rule 70, as Your Honour is aware and as my colleagues, I'm sure, from the Defence are aware, we can only make a request to the Rule 70 provider, and we can ask them to move with alacrity, but ultimately the decision and the decision-making process that is undertaken by the provider sometimes is long and onerous and complex, it has to go through many bureaucratic layers, and we can't expedite that any more than we have already made a request, saying, in some cases when we ask for documents to be provided to us, that it's urgent. We can't do any more than that. So we are taking all the necessary steps that we can to ensure that, one, the Defence gets, as soon as possible, the materials necessary to prepare their Defence, and we are moving as quickly as we can and we are working cooperatively with the Defence to find ways to ensure that they get the materials in a timely fashion. That is what I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Harmon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... privy through Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ms. Featherstone and through the Rule 65 ter conferences what undertakings we have made and what has been produced in the course of this pre-trial phase. We will continue to work --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And we will continue to try to expedite the procedure and find solutions to problems that will confront us in this ongoing process. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just deal with one thing. Mr. Brashich, you were asked to provide the transcripts of the video sequences. Do you have any which you can hand over?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll provide those --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will provide the transcripts of those that have been transcribed to Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In 7 or 14 days, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As soon as I get to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, one final comment, or perhaps question, regarding the pilot project that Mr. Tieger described, and perhaps he can be of assistance to all of us. And the question is this: How many pages are ready for analysis immediately, how many have this draft translation, and how fast will we go through the 5.000 or so untranslated documents? How soon can they be translated in this draft form so that we can work with the language assistants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, I think that's a matter which Mr. Tieger can deal with you directly or through administrative means. I'm glad there has been this level of cooperation, and the Court would encourage it, particularly with a view to starting this trial as soon as possible. Mr. Brashich, is there any matter you want to raise about your client's detention?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there are any other matters, we'll adjourn. The next Status Conference should be fairly shortly after the Prosecution pre-trial brief is delivered. What I'll say at the moment is it should take place during the week of the 6th of May, and we'll fix a date as soon as possible for it. We'll adjourn now.

procedural_notes.text: [Trial Chamber and Senior Legal Officer confer]
--- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
